title: The core concepts in one page
dek: The nine ideas that come up in almost every design: what each one is, when it enters an interview, and what to say about it. Each points to its full article in Concepts.

head: Concept
Comes up when
rows: When you draw the first boxes, choose how the client talks to you, or explain why a response is slow.
Right after the requirements and entities, in the API step: about five minutes.
Twice: name the core entities after the requirements, and sketch a schema when the database enters the design.
When reads are far more than the database can take, a query is slow, or a latency target is tight.
Only when the numbers show one database can't hold the data or take the writes, after a bigger machine, replicas and a cache.
Whenever data or connections are spread over a changing number of servers: caches, key-value stores, chat gateways.
In the non-functional requirements, and again for each feature in the deep dives.
When you name the queries each table must answer, or when a query is too slow.
In the estimates step, and whenever you are about to add a cache, a shard or a queue.
body.label: Where each concept enters an answer

body.x: How a request gets from a phone to your servers and back: DNS, TCP or UDP, TLS, HTTP, the API styles built on it, load balancers at layer 4 or 7, and the distance between regions.

items: Comes up: When you draw the first boxes, choose how the client talks to you, or explain why a response is slow.
Say: Use HTTP and REST unless a requirement says otherwise; use WebSockets or server-sent events only for live updates; put a load balancer in front of every group of servers.
Read: 'Networking essentials' in Concepts.

body.x: Turning the features into calls: resources and methods, what goes in the path, query and body, pagination, idempotency keys, versions and authentication.

items: Comes up: Right after the requirements and entities, in the API step: about five minutes.
Say: One call per feature, REST by default, a cursor for any list that grows, and an idempotency key for anything that charges money or creates something.
Read: 'API design' in Concepts.

body.x: Choosing a database model and shaping the data: entities, keys and relationships, indexes, when to copy data for faster reads, and how to split it later.

items: Comes up: Twice: name the core entities after the requirements, and sketch a schema when the database enters the design.
Say: Start relational; add another kind of store only for a part that needs it, and name the queries each table must answer.
Read: 'Data modelling' in Concepts.

body.x: Keeping copies of hot data closer to whoever reads it: in the app, at the edge (a CDN), in a shared cache such as Redis, or inside the database.

items: Comes up: When reads are far more than the database can take, a query is slow, or a latency target is tight.
Say: Cache-aside with a TTL by default, and one thing that goes wrong (a stampede, stale data, a hot key) with your fix.
Read: 'Caching' in Concepts.

body.x: Splitting the data across machines by a key, so each holds and writes a share.

items: Comes up: Only when the numbers show one database can't hold the data or take the writes, after a bigger machine, replicas and a cache.
Say: The shard key and why it spreads the load evenly, plus what becomes hard: hot keys, queries across shards, transactions across shards.
Read: 'Sharding' in Concepts.

body.x: Placing keys and servers on a ring so that adding or removing a server moves only a small share of the keys.

items: Comes up: Whenever data or connections are spread over a changing number of servers: caches, key-value stores, chat gateways.
Say: With hash(key) % N, changing N moves almost every key; a ring with virtual nodes moves about 1/N and spreads load evenly.
Read: 'Consistent hashing' in Concepts.

body.x: When the network between copies breaks, you choose: refuse some requests to stay consistent, or answer from the copy you have and accept stale data.

items: Comes up: In the non-functional requirements, and again for each feature in the deep dives.
Say: Decide per feature: a seat booking or a payment needs consistency; a feed, a rating or a menu can be a little stale.
Read: 'CAP theorem' in Concepts.

body.x: Sorted structures that find one row without reading the whole table: B-trees, LSM trees, hash indexes, and special ones for places and text.

items: Comes up: When you name the queries each table must answer, or when a query is too slow.
Say: An index for each frequent query, in the right column order, and what each costs: slower writes and more storage.
Read: 'Database indexing' in Concepts.

body.x: What one machine can really do today: memory, disk, a database's reads and writes a second, a cache's operations a second, and how long things take.

items: Comes up: In the estimates step, and whenever you are about to add a cache, a shard or a queue.
Say: Scale only when a number forces it, and say which number it was.
Read: 'Numbers to know' in Concepts.
